btdac.moment: BTDAC receives Bluetooth A2DP audio and sends it over I2S to the PCM5102 DAC. Its line output can connect to an amplifier or powered speakers.
btdac.struggle: The firmware keeps a BLE control channel separate from audio. The Android app can find the device, connect and request test tones. The project guide covers wiring, DAC configuration and power.
whatWorks: Bluetooth A2DP audio reception
Stereo I2S output to the PCM5102
BLE connection from the Android app
Test tone generation through the tone: command
RGB LED indicating connection and playback states
whatDoesnt: The line output requires an amplifier to drive passive speakers
The app controls test tones; remote volume and equalization are not implemented
Battery life depends on the cells and power consumption; no reference measurement has been published

speaker.moment: WiFi Speaker combines network and Bluetooth audio reception on an ESP32. Two MAX98357 I2S amplifiers drive the audio channels, and an LCD shows playback status.
speaker.struggle: The firmware includes WiFi radio, URL streaming and Bluetooth A2DP modes. The web interface lets you select sources and adjust controls. The project is still in development; external services and stream addresses can change.
whatWorks: WiFi radio and URL streaming modes in the firmware
Bluetooth A2DP reception
I2S output to two MAX98357 amplifiers
Web control interface
LCD and mDNS name access on compatible networks
whatDoesnt: Streaming requires an accessible network and audio source
YouTube integration depends on an external Invidious instance
Battery life and usable power depend on the build; no reference tests have been published

hios-node-ai.moment: HIOS Node AI connects an ESP32-S3 to an Ollama server on the local network. Pressing a button sends a preset text query and displays the response on an OLED screen.
hios-node-ai.struggle: A FreeRTOS task handles the HTTP request while the main loop updates the display. The model runs on the server, not the ESP32. The WiFi network, server address and model name are configured in the firmware.
whatWorks: Preset query sent to Ollama’s /api/chat endpoint
Physical button to trigger the query
Status and response shown on an SSD1306 OLED display
HTTP request handled in a FreeRTOS task
HTTP error and WiFi disconnection indications
whatDoesnt: Requires an Ollama server accessible on the local network
The query and credentials are configured before compilation
Voice capture, audio playback and TinyML are not implemented in the current firmware
Response time depends on the server, model and network

pad.moment: HIOS PAD is a programmable desktop controller built around an ESP32-S3 N16R8, a 4-inch TFT display (480 × 320), a diode-isolated 2 × 5 key matrix (true N-Key Rollover), 2 momentary ALT keys, an accelerated rotary encoder, an analog thumb joystick, stereo I2S audio, and 8 NeoPixel LEDs in 2 zones.
pad.struggle: The exact same physical hardware supports two firmware personalities: a desktop Control-Deck (16 shortcut layers, macros, mouse pointer, WiZ/OpenRGB smart lighting, and 4 live PC telemetry monitor views with sparklines via pad-companion) or a one-handed Gaming Keypad / HID Gamepad (360° analog or WASD thumbstick movement, ghost-free diode matrix, and per-genre HUD profiles).
whatWorks: Composite keyboard, mouse and media HID over native USB (TinyUSB) and Bluetooth BLE (NimBLE) with auto-switching
2 × 5 matrix with 1N4148 diodes (ghost-free NKRO), 2 momentary ALT keys (Launcher & Macros) and 2200 Hz I2S acoustic click
3.3 V analog thumbstick with quadratic pointer acceleration, tap left-click, double-tap right-click and NVS calibration
Rotary encoder with dynamic acceleration and double-tap live override (Layer, Volume, Scroll, Zoom, Tabs)
RGB565 Theme Engine (Dark/Light modes + 7 global accent colors + per-layer color on display and dual-zone NeoPixels)
4 full-screen Telemetry Monitor views (General, Network, Cores, Disk) with 56-sample sparklines and flicker-free partial rendering
pad-companion daemon (Windows/Linux) with OS-wide mic mute, UDP WiZ smart light control, live SSE mirror and hot LittleFS web editor
Embedded PWA served directly from ESP32-S3 PROGMEM (http://hiospad.local) with virtual 2 × 5 pad and quick editor
Dual firmware support: Productivity Control-Deck and Gaming Keypad / HID Gamepad on the same hardware
whatDoesnt: Live PC telemetry monitors, WiZ lighting control and OS-wide mic mute require pad-companion running on the local network
The companion includes native Windows and Linux providers; macOS support is pending
ADC battery sensing on GPIO9 is disabled in favor of the NeoPixel data line (actual 2S pack voltage is shown on the LM2596S buck display)

esp32-wroom-32.name: ESP32-WROOM-32 DevKit
esp32-wroom-32.description: Microcontroller with WiFi and Bluetooth 4.2. Board with two rows of 19 pins.
esp32-wroom-32.iface: UART · SPI · I2C · I2S · ADC · DAC

pins.name: IO34 / IO35 / IO36 / IO39
pins.to: **input only**: no output or internal pull resistor

pins.name: ADC2
pins.to: unavailable while WiFi is active (use ADC1)

notes.title: Input-only pins
notes.body: IO34/35/36/39 have no internal pull resistors and cannot act as outputs. Use them for sensors/ADC, not to drive loads.

notes.title: ADC2 and WiFi
notes.body: ADC2 is unavailable with WiFi enabled. If you need ADC with WiFi, use **ADC1** (IO32–39).

esp32-s3-devkitc-1.name: ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1
esp32-s3-devkitc-1.description: Microcontroller with USB OTG, WiFi 802.11 b/g/n and BLE 5. Two rows of 22 pins.
esp32-s3-devkitc-1.iface: USB · UART · SPI · I2C · I2S · LCD

pins.name: 3V3
pins.to: 3.3V regulator rail; external power is also possible according to the board schematic. Do not combine with USB/5V.

pins.name: 5V
pins.to: power input (VBUS or external buck) → LDO → 3V3

pins.name: IO1–IO10
pins.to: ADC1 — preferred with WiFi; ADC2 shares resources with WiFi

pins.name: IO38 o IO48
pins.label: IO38 or IO48
pins.to: onboard WS2812 RGB LED — **depends on the revision**
pins.note: v1.1 → IO38 · v1.0 → IO48. NEVER IO39. Check your board’s silkscreen before using either pin.

pins.name: IO33–IO37
pins.note: used by PSRAM on modules with the R8 suffix

pins.name: IO0 / IO3 / IO45 / IO46
pins.to: strapping (boot) — avoid or use with care

pins.name: demás IOxx
pins.label: other IOxx
pins.to: free GPIO — I2C/SPI/I2S use the flexible GPIO matrix

notes.title: Unavailable PSRAM / flash pins
notes.body: On the **N16R8**, flash uses GPIO **26–32** and octal PSRAM uses **33–37**: these pins are unavailable. The generic S3 datasheet still lists them.

notes.title: I2S/SPI/I2C are flexible
notes.body: The S3 has a GPIO matrix: **any** free pin can carry I2S/SPI/I2C. There is no single “I2S pin”. See the pad build guide for its wiring.

max98357a.name: MAX98357A
max98357a.description: Mono class-D amplifier with I2S input. Check channel selection, power and speaker connections.

pins.name: LRC
pins.to: MCU word select (bus, to both amplifiers)

pins.name: SPK−
pins.note: bridge-tied load (BTL): NEITHER output connects to GND

notes.title: Stereo with 2 modules
notes.body: Both amplifiers share the **same** 3 I2S lines (BCLK/LRC/DIN). Each amplifier’s **SD** pin selects L/R, not a separate data wire.

notes.title: Select the channel (measure SD)
notes.body: Use the SD calculation to choose a resistor for Vin and your board’s pullup. The table shows typical, not guaranteed, thresholds. Measure SD relative to GND; an unconnected GAIN sets 9 dB.

notes.title: Output
notes.body: Connect a 4–8Ω speaker directly to SPK+/SPK− (filterless Class D). Do not connect either output to GND.

pcm5102.name: PCM5102A DAC
pcm5102.description: 32-bit/384kHz I2S DAC (GY-PCM5102 breakout). L/R line output.

pins.name: SCK
pins.note: to GND: the PCM5102 generates its clock using a PLL (no MCU master clock)

notes.title: SCK to GND
notes.body: The breakout receives no master clock from the ESP32: bridge **SCK to GND** so the PCM5102 generates its own clock using its PLL.

notes.title: Jumpers
notes.body: On the back. With all 4 in their default state, the DAC starts playing standard I2S audio.

head: Jumper (back side)
State
rows: L = normal latency · H = low latency
H = no external mute · L = muted

lm2596.name: LM2596 buck (step-down)
lm2596.description: Adjustable step-down DC-DC regulator. Usable current depends on the module and its cooling.

pins.name: IN+
pins.to: from charger/BMS P+ (must exceed output by ~1.5V)

notes.title: Adjust BEFORE connecting the load
notes.body: Turn the potentiometer and **measure OUT+ with a multimeter until it reads 5.0V** before connecting the ESP32/amplifiers. The chip’s 3A rating does not guarantee 3A continuous on every module: check temperature, voltage drop and current with your load.

notes.title: Non-isolated ground
notes.body: IN− and OUT− share the same ground; input and output are not isolated.

jack-trs.name: 3.5mm TRS jack (stereo)
jack-trs.description: Stereo female connector: Tip=L, Ring=R, Sleeve=GND.

pins.name: SW
pins.to: insertion detection (optional, not on every jack)

notes.title: Detection
notes.body: Some jacks add a contact that opens/closes when a plug is inserted.

notes.title: Identify the contacts
notes.body: Tip/Ring/Sleeve describe the audio contacts, not the order of the solder terminals. With a plug inserted and the module unpowered, check continuity to identify each terminal.

plug-trrs.name: Plug 3.5mm TRRS (CTIA)
plug-trrs.description: Male connector with microphone, CTIA standard (modern phones).

notes.title: CTIA vs OMTP
notes.body: CTIA: Ring2=GND, Sleeve=MIC. OMTP swaps them. If the microphone does not work, the standard may be the reason.

ili9488.name: 4-inch TFT ILI9488 (SPI)
ili9488.description: 480×320 SPI display. Supply, backlight and level shifting depend on the module variant.
ili9488.voltage: VCC depends on variant / ESP32 logic 3.3V

pins.name: VCC
pins.to: 5V on the PAD variant with regulator; confirm your module’s range before connecting

pins.name: LED
pins.to: backlight / brightness control (depends on module; see note)

pins.name: T_CS
pins.to: touch: chip select (unused in the pad)

notes.title: Write only
notes.body: In the PAD, MISO (SDO) is unconnected (`TFT_MISO=-1`). Depending on the board, LED may be a logic control or the backlight supply: check the schematic and use a driver if it carries load current. Do not power the backlight directly from a GPIO.

notes.title: Touch
notes.body: The touch controller (T_CLK/T_CS/T_DIN/T_DO/T_IRQ) uses the same header but the pad does not use it. Some units also have a microSD slot with separate pins.

lcd1602-i2c.name: LCD 16×2 I2C (HD44780 + PCF8574)
lcd1602-i2c.description: 16×2 character display with I2C backpack: only 2 data pins.

notes.title: I2C address
notes.body: PCF8574: **0x20–0x27**; PCF8574A: **0x38–0x3F**. A0/A1/A2 set the address. Scan the bus instead of assuming 0x27.

notes.title: Contrast
notes.body: Blue potentiometer on the back of the backpack.

notes.title: I2C with ESP32
notes.body: Many backpacks have SDA/SCL pull-ups to **5V**. Use a bidirectional level shifter between the 5V backpack and the 3.3V ESP32. Do not connect lines with 5V pull-ups directly to the MCU.

ky-040.name: KY-040 rotary encoder
ky-040.description: Incremental encoder with push button. On-board pull-ups.

notes.title: Power at 3V3 with the S3
notes.body: The module has pull-ups: powering it at 5V puts 5V on the ESP32-S3 GPIOs. Use **3V3**.

notes.title: Reading
notes.body: CLK/DT in quadrature; SW with `INPUT_PULLUP` (active low).

hw-504.name: HW-504 analog joystick
hw-504.description: PlayStation-style joystick: 2 analog axes + push button.

pins.name: +5V
pins.note: 5V overvolts the S3 ADC and couples the axes (diagonal)

notes.title: Power at 3V3
notes.body: The pin says “+5V”, but connect it to **3V3** on the ESP32-S3. At 5V the wiper overvolts the ADC pins, making the protection diode conduct and coupling the two axes.

ws2812.name: WS2812 / SK6812 strip (NeoPixel)
ws2812.description: Chained addressable RGB LEDs: the whole strip uses 1 data pin.

pins.name: DOUT
pins.to: to the next LED’s DIN (daisy chain)

notes.title: 3.3 → 5V level shifting
notes.body: With a **5V** strip and a **3.3V** ESP32, use a **74AHCT125** to level-shift DIN. Threshold and current depend on the LED revision; replacing WS2812 with SK6812 does not guarantee 3.3V compatibility.

notes.title: Power supply
notes.body: 330Ω in series with DIN + a 470–1000µF capacitor on the strip’s 5V rail. Limit brightness to protect the buck converter.

ky-009.name: KY-009 LED RGB (SMD)
ky-009.description: Common-cathode RGB LED. NO on-board resistors.

notes.title: No resistors
notes.body: The module has NO resistors: add **330Ω in series** with each color or you will damage the LED.

notes.title: Common cathode
notes.body: The `−` pin is common GND; the colors are driven by active-high PWM.

charger-2s.name: 2S USB-C charger / BMS
charger-2s.description: Connection reference for 2S modules. Charging, balancing and protection depend on the specific model.

notes.title: 2S = series
notes.body: B+/BM/B− connect to the 2 cells **in series** (2S, 6.0–8.4V). BM (balance) is essential for even charging.

notes.title: Output
notes.body: P+/P− are the load terminals of the illustrated module. Not every BMS includes a charger, balancing or simultaneous load management: verify these functions in your model’s documentation. USB-C alone does not guarantee them.

holder-2s.name: 18650 2S cell holder (series)
holder-2s.description: Holder for two 18650 cells in series (2S). Verify that the wiring is in series.

pins.name: mid
pins.to: midpoint between cells → BM; needed if the BMS requires a balancing connection

notes.title: Series, not parallel
notes.body: For 2S, the 2 cells connect **in series** (voltages add). A parallel holder would provide 3.7V, not 7.4V.

notes.title: Balancing
notes.body: Connect the midpoint to the charger’s BM pin so the cells charge evenly.

voiceLatency.title: Voice latency estimator
voiceLatency.description: Compare scenarios by adding end-of-speech detection, transcription, network, first-token and speech synthesis times. These are illustrative values, not product measurements.
voiceLatency.scope: Measure each stage on the target device and network. This calculator adds times sequentially; it does not run speech recognition, synthesis or audio playback.
voiceLatency.streaming: Streaming can overlap stages. To evaluate it, measure when audio starts and how the response continues, as well as the total time.
voiceLatency.tuning: End-of-speech thresholds and chunk size affect waiting time and phrase boundaries. Adjust them using representative recordings and tests.
voiceLatency.done: Simulation complete; no audio was generated.
voiceLatency.hintFast: The sum is below half a second. The actual experience needs measurement of the complete system.
voiceLatency.hintMedium: Compare each stage’s contribution to identify where to reduce the wait.
voiceLatency.hintSlow: The sum approaches or exceeds one second. Compare these durations with device measurements.
voiceLatency.hintLong: Check which stage contributes the most time. This result describes the scenario, not a performance measurement.

vram.title: Memory scenarios for local models
vram.description: Compare sizes and formats with a simplified formula. Profiles are illustrative scenarios; they do not describe an exact model architecture or guarantee that it will load.
vram.offload: GPU layers assigned in the example

vram.cpuTitle: The scenario assigns layers to RAM
vram.cpuBody: The formula totals {total} GB of weights and cache and allocates {ram} GB to RAM. Change context or format to compare.
vram.ramTitle: The calculation exceeds the specified RAM
vram.ramBody: The result is {needed} GB against {available} GB specified. This is not a load test or a measurement of your computer.
vram.scope: Weights are approximated as parameters × bits / 8. The cache uses a fixed coefficient of 0.0003 multiplied by context and model size, adjusted by the format factor; it does not use the actual architecture. The calculation reserves 0.6 GB for the engine. Results let you explore this formula, not select hardware or confirm compatibility. Adapt file names, models and command options, then measure usage with your engine.

The example waits for WiFi at startup and does not include a complete reconnection or task synchronization strategy. Code comments and status messages are in English. pad.title: PAD software: controls, editor and companion
pad.description: Configure PAD actions and organize them by context. The firmware provides USB and Bluetooth controls; the companion adds web editing and communication with Windows or Linux.

controls.title: Layers, shortcuts and mouse control
controls.body: Ten action keys and two ALT keys organize shortcuts by context. The encoder controls volume, scrolling or zoom depending on the layer; the joystick moves the pointer. USB and BLE send keyboard, mouse and media actions. WiFi is used for configuration and companion communication.

editor.title: Your configuration, without rebuilding
editor.body: The companion web editor changes layers, actions, text and macros, including Windows and Linux shortcut variants. It saves the editable configuration and sends the current operating system variant to PAD. A web mirror displays the device interface. Adapt the same hardware to editing, development, browsing or meetings.

companion.title: Real computer state
companion.body: The companion reads volume and microphone state, plus CPU/GPU load and temperature when sensors are available. It sends feedback to PAD over the local network and can toggle global microphone mute. Camera controls and some meeting shortcuts depend on the active application.

setup.title: Getting started
setup.body: Start with PAD over USB or BLE using its firmware layers. To add feedback and web editing, build the companion following its README, configure the PAD address and firmware-generated token, and run it on the same network. Windows includes login installation; Linux documents a systemd user service.

availability.title: What works independently
availability.body: HID shortcuts and controls work without a companion or WiFi. Real feedback and global microphone mute require the companion. Windows and Linux providers are implemented; macOS is not yet supported. Sensor readings depend on your hardware. Global camera mute is not implemented in the companion.

btdac.title: BTDAC: Bluetooth audio and test tools

audio.title: From Bluetooth to your DAC
audio.body: The ESP32 acts as an A2DP receiver for audio from a phone or computer. RGB LEDs indicate waiting, connection, playback and errors. The BLE control channel is independent of the Bluetooth connection used for music.

android.title: Test tones from Android
android.body: The Kotlin application built with Jetpack Compose scans for the HIOS BTDAC BLE service, lets you select and connect a device, and sends frequency commands. Firmware generates stereo sine tones from 20 Hz to 20 kHz for approximately two seconds. It does not start a tone while music is playing.

setup.title: Getting started
setup.body: Build and flash the firmware following the BTDAC documentation. Pair an audio source to listen to music. For test tones, build the Android application from source, grant Bluetooth permissions and connect to BTDAC inside the application. No account or cloud service is required.

availability.title: Current scope
availability.body: The app lets you request test tones. Remote volume and equalization, battery monitoring and OTA updates are planned. The Android app is distributed as source code to build with Android Studio or Gradle.

speaker.description: The Speaker firmware plays WiFi radio, YouTube audio and Bluetooth A2DP over I2S to dual MAX98357A amplifiers in stereo, with local web control and chiptune song playback.

modes.title: WiFi Radio, Bluetooth A2DP and Chiptune Player
modes.body: The ESP32 switches seamlessly between HTTP radio streams, Bluetooth Classic A2DP audio, and direct chiptune playback using .device.json files exported from the HIOS Chiptune Composer.

streaming.title: Local Web Control and Wireless Configuration
streaming.body: Once connected to your local network, the device serves a web control dashboard at http://hios-speaker.local to change stations, adjust volume, and upload new songs via HTTP POST /api/song. It also supports WiFi configuration via Bluetooth Serial terminal.

setup.title: Getting started
setup.body: Adjust the LM2596 buck converter to 5.0 V with a multimeter before connecting modules. Flash the testbench diagnostic firmwares first to verify the I2S bus and stereo separation, then compile and flash src/main.ino with PlatformIO.

availability.title: Current scope
availability.body: Native stereo output at 44.1 kHz / 16-bit using dual MAX98357A class-D amplifiers with hardware L/R channel selection via resistors on SD pins. The 16×2 LCD connected over I2C displays connection status, IP address, and current title without external cloud services.

pad.intro: The PAD groups shortcuts into layers and displays their labels. USB or BLE carries keyboard, mouse and media controls; the companion adds web editing and real computer state.

steps.1: Connect the ESP32-S3 native USB port to your PC for HID, or pair over BLE. Try Copy and Paste in a test document.
steps.2: Press the encoder to open the menu, turn it to browse groups and press a key to select a layer. Its function changes with the layer; the joystick moves the pointer.
steps.3: Start the companion on the same network as the PAD. Open the editor, change a label or action and choose Save + restart to send it to the device.

pad.board: For ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 N16R8 (16 MB flash, 8 MB OPI PSRAM) with an ILI9488 display. Keep the project configuration; this firmware is not for the DAC’s classic ESP32.
pad.connect: With the 2S battery pack connected, open SW-CELDAS before plugging in USB. Use UART/CH343 for flashing and logs; native USB is used for HID.
pad.success: At startup, the serial monitor prints the API/OTA token: keep it for companion configuration. Then test controls over native USB. See the full guide for OTA and recovery.

pad.companionSetup: For real use: run npm install and npm run build in projects/pad/companion, copy config.example.json to config.json and set host and token. Run npm start. Default URLs: http://localhost:8787 for the mirror and http://localhost:8787/admin.html for the editor. Windows and Linux providers are implemented; macOS is pending.

btdac.intro: The DAC receives music over Bluetooth A2DP and sends stereo line audio through PCM5102. The Android app uses a separate BLE channel for test tones.

steps.1: Connect the line output to an amplifier or powered speakers and turn on the DAC. Start at low volume.
steps.2: Find HIOS BTDAC in your phone or PC Bluetooth settings, pair and play music. Audio playback does not need the Android app.
steps.3: Build android/ with Android Studio, grant Bluetooth permissions and connect in the app. Stop music before requesting a tone; it lasts about two seconds.

btdac.board: For classic ESP32 (esp32dev / WROOM-32) with PCM5102. ESP32-S3 is not a replacement for this A2DP firmware.
btdac.connect: Check power and PCM5102 wiring before connecting the ESP32 programming USB port.
btdac.success: After uploading, open the serial monitor at 115200 and find HIOS BTDAC over Bluetooth. If it connects without sound, follow the full guide’s SCK, XSMT and I2S checks. Build Android from source; no APK or firmware binary is provided here.

speaker.intro: The speaker plays WiFi radio streams, Bluetooth A2DP audio, and chiptunes from the Composer, outputting stereo I2S audio to dual MAX98357A amplifiers and a 16×2 LCD.

steps.1: Adjust the LM2596 buck converter to 5.0 V with a multimeter before connecting modules. Check GND continuity across all boards.
steps.2: Flash 01_power_i2s_smoke.ino first to validate the I2S bus, then 02_channel_check_lr.ino to verify left and right channel separation.
steps.3: Flash src/main.ino, open http://hios-speaker.local in your browser to configure your stations or pair your phone over Bluetooth A2DP.

speaker.board: For classic ESP32 (esp32dev / WROOM-32 configuration) with 2× MAX98357A and 16×2 LCD. Do not use ESP32-S3 as it lacks Bluetooth Classic A2DP.
speaker.connect: Wire the shared I2S bus: DIN to GPIO25, BCLK to GPIO26, and LRC to GPIO27. Verify SD pin resistors (100 kΩ for left, 220 kΩ for right) and clean 5V power.
speaker.success: On boot, the 16×2 LCD displays the assigned IP address and active mode. Control playback and volume from http://hios-speaker.local or over serial.

Qpsk.title: QPSK MODULATION AND I/Q CONSTELLATION
Qpsk.noise: AWGN noise: σ per I/Q component
Qpsk.pauseHint: Pause or 0.0x freezes phase and noise. Editing parameters recalculates the views using the same samples.
Qpsk.tapHint: Click a column or use the symbol buttons to change the dibit.
Qpsk.timeCanvas: I and Q channels and the ideal transmitted QPSK signal, without noise or filtering.
Qpsk.constellationCanvas: Normalized symbol constellation with AWGN; connecting lines are geometric guides.
Qpsk.phaseExplanation: 00 → 11 changes from 45° to 225° relative to the gray cosine: a 180° difference between symbols, not relative to the reference. Red markers indicate any phase change, including 90°.
Qpsk.trajectoryExplanation: The line joining opposite symbols passes through (0,0), but it is a geometric guide. It does not simulate a filtered transition or demonstrate that the CH3 envelope reaches zero.
Qpsk.noiseExplanation: σ is the noise standard deviation in each normalized component. Es = 1, N₀ = 2σ² and theoretical BER = ½ erfc(1/(2σ)), assuming ideal quadrant decisions and no coding. There is no universal noise threshold.
Qpsk.modelLimits: CH3 shows the ideal transmission; noise is applied only to constellation symbols. CH3 is not demodulated and BER is not measured. The model does not include optical OSNR, filters, FEC or amplifiers. At σ = 0, Es/N₀ = ∞ and theoretical BER = 0.
Qpsk.referenceDescription: I/Q convention, Gray mapping, AWGN noise and model limitations.

rc.title: RC oscilloscope
rc.description: Input and output voltage of an ideal RC low-pass filter, on the same time and voltage scales.
rc.hint: Sine-wave steady state, ideal source and unloaded output. At fc: −3.01 dB and −45°. Changes to R or C recalculate steady state; switching transients are not modeled.

i2s.title: I²S clock laboratory
i2s.description: Upper trace: bit clock. Lower trace: word select. Ideal logic levels 0 and 1, displayed on separate lanes.
i2s.hint: Stereo bus: BCLK = fs × 2 × slot bits; WS = fs. Upper lane: BCLK. Lower lane: WS (0 = left, 1 = right). Logic levels are not voltages. This is a local simulation, not a reading from the board.
i2s.dataHint: Slot width can exceed audio bit depth. DIN and MCLK are not drawn. In standard I²S, the next word’s MSB follows the WS change by one BCLK period.
i2s.invalid: Enter a positive sample rate and 16, 24 or 32-bit slots. When configuring audio, its precision must fit in the slot and all other parameters must be valid.

gain.title: Non-inverting amplifier oscilloscope
gain.description: Input and output voltage of an ideal non-inverting amplifier, on the same time scale and a shared automatic voltage scale.
gain.schematic: Non-inverting amplifier: Vin at the positive input, Rf from Vout to the negative input, and Rg from the negative input to ground.
gain.hint: Av = 1 + Rf/Rg; Vout = Av × Vin, with φ = 0°. Increasing Rf increases gain; increasing Rg reduces it. Rf = 0 gives unity gain. Both channels share an automatic voltage scale. Ideal steady-state model: no supply-rail clipping, bandwidth limit or slew-rate limit.
gain.invalid: Use finite values: Rf ≥ 0, Rg > 0, and positive input frequency and amplitude. The resulting voltage must also fit the numeric range.

rl.title: RL oscilloscope
rl.description: Input voltage and output voltage across R of an ideal RL low-pass filter, on the same time and voltage scales.
rl.hint: Vout is measured across R: H = R / (R + jωL). At fc: −3.01 dB and −45°. Sinusoidal steady state, ideal source and no additional output load; transients and inductor losses are not modeled.

rcl.title: Series RLC oscilloscope
rcl.description: Input voltage and output voltage across R of an ideal series RLC circuit. Vout = VR, on the same time and voltage scales.
rcl.schematic: Series RLC circuit: input Vin, output Vout across R relative to ground.
rcl.hint: Vout = VR: H = R / [R + j(ωL − 1/ωC)]. This is a band-pass response: at f0, |Z| is minimum, Vout = Vin and φ = 0°. Below f0 the output leads; above it, the output lags. Uses the calculator frequency f. Steady state with R > 0, an ideal source and no additional load; transients and parasitic losses are excluded.

max.assumptions: Internal pulldown: 100 kΩ ±8%. The calculation assumes pullup resistors connect to Vin; check the schematic if your board uses another connection. Leave GAIN unconnected for 9 dB. Measure SD relative to GND.
max.intro: Both MAX98357A modules share BCLK, LRC and DIN. SD selects the channel; an unconnected GAIN sets 9 dB. Example at 5 V with no onboard pullup.
max.singleTitle: One module: connections and channel selection
max.stereoTitle: Two modules on the same I²S bus

max.speaker: 4–8 Ω speaker
max.measureHint: Use the SD calculation and verify the channel.

steps: Identify any onboard resistor between SD and Vin. Enter it in the calculation: it is in parallel with the external resistor.
Leave GAIN unconnected for 9 dB. An unconnected SD without a pullup is pulled down internally and shuts the amplifier down.
Right example at 5 V without an onboard pullup: {resistance} kΩ ±5% to Vin gives about {voltage} V. Left: connect SD directly to Vin.
Verify the supply rail before connecting. Measure SD with the red probe and GND with the black probe.
For Right, the guaranteed window between thresholds is {min}–{max} V. The calculation also accounts for resistor tolerances.
At 5 V, 220 kΩ without an additional pullup gives about 1.56 V nominally: it is not a valid Right recommendation. Repeat the measurement on both modules.

pad.meta_subtitle: ESP32-S3 macropad: 4" ILI9488 display, direct navigation (ALT×2 + encoder + joystick), 10 actions in a 2×5 matrix, 8 NeoPixels and 2 I2S speakers.
pad.meta_note: Wiring matches firmware rev 0.9 (scanned 2×5 matrix + I2S bus). The self-test checks this guide against Pins.h and platformio.ini on every run.
pad.module_power_power: 2S cells → SW-CELDAS → 5.0V buck (≥3A) → 5V rail · S3 5V pin → onboard LDO → 3V3 rail
pad.module_power_tip: Measure **5.0V** at the buck output **before** connecting the S3. The DevKit generates 3V3 itself (SGM2212-3.3 LDO, 800mA): **do not supply it externally**.
pad.module_display_power: VCC → 5V · GND → GND · LED → SW-PANTALLA → GPIO21
pad.module_display_tip: The ILI9488 uses **3.3V** logic (IOVCC absolute maximum 3.3V), matching the GPIOs. **Check for a 74HC245 buffer** near the header: powered from module VCC at 5V, its input threshold is 3.5V, above the 3.3V SPI signal, causing a **blank display**. For that module, connect VCC to **3V3**, not 5V.
pad.module_matrix_power: No supply: each key closes COLUMN → diode → ROW
pad.module_matrix_tip: 2 OUTPUT rows (driven LOW one at a time) + 5 INPUT_PULLUP columns. One diode per key, **cathode (stripe) toward the ROW**. Without diodes, pressing 3 keys can cause ghosting.
pad.module_nav_power: No supply: button directly to GND (INPUT_PULLUP)
pad.module_nav_tip: These buttons sit **outside** the matrix, **without diodes**. They open layers/menus and must always be readable.
pad.module_stick_tip: The module pin marked "+5V" connects to **3V3**. At 5V it overvolts the S3 ADC and the axes couple near their upper limit. Both axes use GPIO1/GPIO2 = **ADC1**, which remains available with WiFi/BLE enabled.
pad.module_audio_tip: Shared I2S bus: all 3 signals connect to **both** amplifiers. Only **SD** differs to select the channel. Filterless class D: connect each 4–8Ω speaker directly, without a filter.
pad.module_led_power: VCC → 5V (or series 1N400x, see note) · GND → GND
pad.module_led_tip: Chain the **2 boards of 4 LEDs on one pin**: first DOUT → second DIN. Each WS2812B has its own controller, so all 8 pixels remain individually addressable (`NEOPIXEL_COUNT=8`). WS2812B requires V_IH = 0.7×VDD = **3.5V**, above the 3.3V GPIO: **outside specification**. A series **1N400x** silicon diode (~0.65V) on strip VCC gives approximately 4.35V and a 3.05V threshold. Alternatively use a 74AHCT125. SK6812 is **not** a guaranteed fix: its typical threshold is still 3.4V.
pad.module_system_power: No wiring: used by the board
pad.module_system_tip: Reserved for USB HID (19/20) and wired programming (43/44). Do not assign these pins to other peripherals.
pad.pin_8_note: ADC1_7, used here as digital input
pad.pin_9_note: Former battery divider input. Battery measurement was removed: do NOT enable BATTERY_ENABLED without reassigning the ADC.
pad.pin_19_dest: Native USB (HID) — RESERVED, do not solder
pad.pin_20_dest: Native USB (HID) — RESERVED, do not solder
pad.pin_21_dest: TFT LED (LEDC PWM) · SW-PANTALLA in series here
pad.pin_38_note: On DevKitC-1 **v1.1**, this pin also drives the onboard RGB LED. Its DIN is high impedance, so scanning works, but the pixel will flash.
pad.pin_41_dest: → LRC of BOTH MAX98357A (L/R word select)
pad.pin_42_dest: → DIN of BOTH MAX98357A (serial data). S3 output DOUT → amplifier input DIN.
pad.pin_48_note: On DevKitC-1 **v1.0**, this pin drives the onboard RGB LED. The button still works; the LED is unused.
pad.rail_c5_c: → ESP32 5V pin · TFT VCC · NeoPixel VCC · 2× MAX98357A Vin · bulk capacitor · **≥3A** buck
pad.rail_c33_c: → Joystick VCC · Encoder + . Generated by onboard SGM2212-3.3 (800mA): **NO external supply**
pad.rail_cg_c: → Battery− · buck · S3 · TFT · joystick · encoder · matrix · ALT · amplifiers · NeoPixel (one common ground)
pad.section_0_ascii:
2S charger ──┬── 2 cells (7.0–8.4V usable)
              └─[SW-CELDAS]─► Buck 5.0V (≥3A) ─► RAIL 5V
   RAIL 5V ─► ESP32 pin 5V ─►(LDO SGM2212)─► pin 3V3 ─► RAIL 3V3
   RAIL 5V ─► cap 470–1000µF ─► GND   (+1000µF near amplifiers)
   RAIL 5V ─► Display VCC ; NeoPixel + 2× amplifier Vin
   GPIO21 ─[SW-PANTALLA]─► Display LED/BL (switch here, NOT VCC!)
   RAIL 3V3 ─► Stick VCC + Encoder + ; Common GND: ALL
pad.section_0_tip: **USB supplies no power** in wireless use. The S3 generates 3V3; do not inject it. Estimated full-load budget: 2 amplifiers at 4Ω (~1.5A) + 8 NeoPixels at white (~0.5A) + S3 RF and backlight (~0.6A) ≈ **2.6A**. Allow margin with a **≥3A** buck.
pad.section_1_tip: **SW-PANTALLA must interrupt LED/BL, not display VCC.** Cutting VCC while GPIO10–14 still carry 3.3V SPI exceeds the ILI9488 input limit (`VIN ≤ IOVCC + 0.3V`, only 0.3V when off). Current through protection diodes can damage it. Keep the module powered and switch the backlight separately.
pad.section_1_row_1_to: Disconnects GPIO21 → display LED/BL (logic stays powered)
pad.section_2_tip: **HSPI** at 27MHz. **Leave MISO disconnected** (`TFT_MISO=-1`): write-only. The 5 signal pins come from `platformio.ini`; backlight is in `Pins.h` and uses LEDC. **CS is GPIO10**: an older document said 13, which would short it to DC.
pad.section_2_row_6_note: With a 74HC245 buffer by the header, use VCC = 3V3 to avoid a blank display
pad.section_3_ascii:
COL0    COL1    COL2    COL3    COL4
        GPIO18  GPIO8   GPIO38  GPIO39  GPIO47
          │       │       │       │       │
ROW0 ────┼─ACC1──┼─ACC2──┼─ACC3──┼─ACC4──┼─ACC5
GPIO15    │       │       │       │       │
          │       │       │       │       │
ROW1 ────┼─ACC6──┼─ACC7──┼─ACC8──┼─ACC9──┼─ACC10
GPIO16

  each key:  COLUMN ──[switch]──|>|── ROW
                                  diode
                          (STRIPE toward ROW)
pad.section_3_tip: 2 **OUTPUT** rows (idle HIGH, driven LOW one at a time) + 5 **INPUT_PULLUP** columns. One diode per key, **cathode (stripe) toward the ROW**. Without diodes, 3 keys in an L can register a fourth (ghosting). If a key fails, check diode orientation. Use 1N4148 or silicon 1N400x/1N540x; **not LEDs**.
pad.section_3_row_3_note: ADC1_7, used here as digital input
pad.section_3_row_4_note: DevKitC-1 v1.1: onboard RGB LED flashes during scanning (cosmetic)
pad.section_4_tip: Deliberately **outside the matrix and without diodes**: these buttons open layers/menus and must **always** be readable, independently of row scanning. Normally open button directly to GND, using the internal pull-up.
pad.section_4_row_1_note: DevKitC-1 v1.0: shared with onboard RGB LED; button still works
pad.section_5_tip: CLK and DT use **interrupts** (quadrature: edge order gives direction). SW is the shaft button: **press to open the menu**. Swap CLK and DT if rotation is reversed. The KY-040 includes pull-ups.
pad.section_6_tip: The pin marked **"+5V" connects to 3V3**. 5V overvolts the S3 ADC and couples the axes near their upper limit. GPIO1/GPIO2 use **ADC1**, available with WiFi/BLE enabled. The joystick button provides the click.
pad.section_6_row_3_note: Ignore the supply label: verify with a meter before power-on
pad.section_7_ascii:
┌────────────────┐
  GPIO40 BCLK ──┬─►│ MAX98357A  L   │──► speaker L (4–8Ω)
  GPIO41 LRC  ──┼─►│ SD → Vin       │
  GPIO42 DOUT ──┼─►│ (DIN)          │
                │  └────────────────┘
                │  ┌────────────────┐
                └─►│ MAX98357A  R   │──► speaker R (4–8Ω)
                   │ SD → {sdResistance}k → Vin│
                   │ (DIN)          │
                   └────────────────┘
       same 3 signals to both · only SD resistor differs
pad.section_7_tip: All **3 lines connect in parallel to both amplifiers**; there is no separate bus per channel. Only **SD** differs to select the channel (see below). **DOUT** at the S3 connects to **DIN** at the amplifier: the same wire.
pad.section_7_row_1_to: → LRC of BOTH amplifiers (L/R time slots)
pad.section_8_tip: MAX98357A **SD** controls both shutdown **and** channel selection through its voltage. The internal **100k** pull-down forms a divider with the resistor to Vin. Thresholds are **absolute voltages**, not fractions of Vdd.
pad.section_8_row_1_note: Example at 5V without an onboard pull-up. If present, use the SD calculator: it is in parallel.
pad.section_9_tip: Speakers have no GPIO: connect each to its amplifier output. MAX98357A is **filterless class D**: connect **directly**, without a filter or coupling capacitor. **Do not test with a resistor** as a dummy load: the unfiltered PWM bridge needs speaker inductance; a resistor dissipates it as heat. **Neither terminal goes to GND**: the output is differential (bridged); grounding it can destroy the amplifier.
pad.section_10_ascii:
GPIO9 ──[330Ω]──► DIN ┌─board A─┐ DOUT ──► DIN ┌─board B─┐
                        │ 0  1    │              │ 4  5    │
                        │ 2  3    │              │ 6  7    │
                        └─────────┘              └─────────┘
   RAIL 5V ──[1N400x]──► VCC of both (~4.35V)
   GND ─────────────────► GND of both

   1 data wire = 8 individually addressable pixels
pad.section_10_tip: The 2 boards share **one data pin** (DOUT A → DIN B). Each WS2812B consumes its first 24 bits, so all 8 pixels are individually addressable (`NEOPIXEL_COUNT=8`). Zone effects are **software**: color 0–3 and 4–7 differently. GPIO9 (former battery input) leaves UART0 (43/44) available for serial/programming without boot flashing. For **per-key feedback**, chain 1 LED per key on the same GPIO9 and increase `NEOPIXEL_COUNT`.
pad.section_10_row_0_to: GPIO9 → series 330Ω → DIN of first board
pad.section_10_row_0_note: 3.3V is below threshold: series 1N400x on VCC, or 74AHCT125
pad.section_10_row_1_note: One direction: DIN→DOUT. Reversing it disables B
pad.section_10_row_2_note: ~60mA/LED at full power: 8 white LEDs ≈ 0.5A. Limit brightness
pad.section_11_tip: Reserved: **do not solder anything here**. GPIO19/20 provide native USB HID; using them breaks PC control. GPIO43/44 are UART0 → CH343 for serial and wired programming. Keep **BOOT (GPIO0)** and native USB-C accessible with the enclosure closed for recovery if OTA fails.
pad.section_11_row_4_to: Recovery after failed OTA — keep accessible
pad.section_12_tip: Battery measurement is disabled: the **power module display** already shows the 2S input voltage. GPIO9 now drives NeoPixel. Keep `BATTERY_ENABLED=false`: `BAT_ADC_PIN` still points to 9. Reconnecting the old divider would put 2.7V DC on the NeoPixel data line.
pad.section_13_tip: Action matrix 7 (2 rows + 5 columns) + 2 direct ALT + 3 I2S = 12 remaining GPIOs used. Only **GPIO3** is free, a strapping pin (JTAG_SEL). Unavailable: **26–32** flash, **33–37** R8 octal PSRAM (DevKitC-1 does not expose 26–34; 35/36/37 are on the header but occupied), 19/20 USB, 43/44 UART0, **0/45/46** strapping (0 is recovery BOOT).
pad.section_13_row_0_to: Strapping (JTAG_SEL): usable as output, leave unloaded during boot
pad.section_13_row_1_to: On header but used by octal PSRAM — using them causes boot loops
pad.section_13_row_2_to: Strapping: selects boot mode. 0 = BOOT, reserved
pad.section_14_tip: A second data pin is unnecessary: the 2 boards already provide **8 individually addressable pixels** on GPIO9. Their equal colors come from **firmware**: `leds::setLayerColor()` iterates over `NEOPIXEL_COUNT` with the same color. Change that loop for different zones (board A ≠ board B), without rewiring. A separate bus would consume the last free pin, **GPIO3** (strapping).

speaker.meta_note: Firmware wiring reference. Verify SD voltage for channel selection. The firmware's 100k/100k battery divider is unsafe for a fully charged 2S pack; redesign and recalibrate before connecting GPIO34.
speaker.module_power_tip: Use a 2–3A or higher buck: both amplifiers draw high peak current.
speaker.module_audio_tip: Shared I2S bus: all 3 signals go to both amplifiers. Each SD pin selects its channel: **measure it**, do not assume.
speaker.module_lcd_tip: PCF8574 backpack at 0x27. Check pull-up voltage; ESP32 I2C signals must not be pulled to 5V.
speaker.module_battery_power: Firmware reference: 100k/100k → GPIO34. DO NOT connect to a 2S pack: 8.4V → 4.2V.
speaker.pin_34_note: GPIO34 is input-only. At 8.4V, this divider gives 4.2V: do not connect it to the ESP32 ADC.
speaker.rail_c5_c: → ESP32 VIN · 2× MAX98357 Vin · LCD VCC · LM2596 (≥2–3A buck)
speaker.rail_cg_c: → ESP32 · amplifiers · LCD · buck · BMS (one common ground)

speaker.section_0_tip: Speakers increase peak current: use a **≥2–3A** buck and bulk capacitance. **Do not connect the firmware's 100k/100k divider to a 2S pack**: 8.4V becomes 4.2V at GPIO34. Select a divider for the ADC range and tolerances, then update the firmware scale and calibration.
speaker.section_1_tip: PCF8574 backpack at **0x27** (sometimes 0x3F). VCC = 5V; rear potentiometer sets contrast. Check the backpack pull-ups: use appropriate I2C level shifting if SDA/SCL are pulled to 5V; do not connect 5V logic directly to ESP32.

Assembly.title: Wiring and assembly bench
Assembly.intro: Work on one module at a time. Explore each signal and record the checks you performed on your build.
Assembly.functional: Functional diagram: numbered terminals identify connections in this list, not physical positions. Power rails and intermediate components are described above and in each signal detail.
Assembly.noSignals: This module has no GPIO signals. Follow the power connections shown above.
Assembly.unpowered: Disconnect USB, power supplies and battery before wiring, soldering or checking continuity. Do not solder directly onto lithium cells.
Assembly.prepareBody: Check the variant and silkscreen against the guide. Identify each endpoint in Wiring, cut and strip wires, prepare insulation and secure the parts. Check polarity and orientation before soldering.
Assembly.solderBody: Use fume extraction and an iron stand. With a clean, tinned tip, heat the terminal and pad together and feed solder into the joint. Remove the solder, then the tip; let it cool without moving. Insulate exposed conductors and secure wires so they do not pull on the pad.
Assembly.inspectBody: Use magnification to check that solder wets both terminal and pad, without bridges or loose strands. With power disconnected, check continuity of each connection and absence of shorts between rails. Visual inspection does not replace these measurements. Complete the project checklist before applying power.

CloudflareTraffic.title: Infrastructure traffic · Cloudflare
CloudflareTraffic.methodology: Aggregates of requests Cloudflare already processes to serve openhios.dev. This source is independent of voluntary usage statistics: their counts are not added together. Imports retain only daily counts and data transfer, without IPs, accounts, cookies, paths or content.
CloudflareTraffic.period: Historical coverage: {from} → {to}. Imported: {updated}. Updated through an explicit import; this is not a live counter.
CloudflareTraffic.limitations: We exclude every verified bot category present in the query. The available plan cannot classify the remaining traffic by bot score: it may include unknown automation, tests and our own traffic. Values are adaptive sample estimates, not people. HTML counts successful 2xx HTML responses; it does not measure client navigation or local tool use.
CloudflareTraffic.partial: The first and last days may be incomplete. Zero means the query returned no activity in its sample; it does not prove that there was no traffic.
